questions: Have you noticed drooping of either upper eyelid?
Does the drooping become worse when you are tired or later in the day?
Does the drooping improve after resting or sleeping?
Do you have difficulty swallowing food or liquids?
Does food or liquid ever come out through your nose?
Does your voice become weak, nasal, or slurred after prolonged speaking?
Do you tire quickly while chewing?
Do you have weakness in your neck, arms, or legs?
Do you have difficulty breathing, especially when lying down or at night?
Do you have numbness or weakness on one side of your body?
Have you had severe headache, dizziness, or loss of balance with these symptoms?
Have you had any recent injury, infection, or surgery before this began?
Have you ever had similar episodes in the past?
Do you have diabetes, high blood pressure, or a history of stroke?
Have you been diagnosed with myasthenia gravis or another nerve or muscle disorder?
Are you taking any new medicines or drugs?
orders: Bedside examination of eyelid fatigability, sustained upgaze, ocular movements, pupils, facial strength, neck flexion, and proximal limb strength
Ice-pack test applied to the more ptotic eyelid
Serum acetylcholine-receptor antibody panel, including binding, blocking, and modulating antibodies
Repetitive nerve-stimulation electromyography of facial and proximal limb muscles
Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine levels
Serum electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal function, and liver function
MRI of the brain and orbits with attention to the ocular motor nerves and extraocular muscles
CT scan of the chest with contrast
Mitochondrial myopathy genetic testing if neuromuscular-junction studies and antibody testing are unrevealing
results: 1. Bedside examination of eyelid fatigability, sustained upgaze, ocular movements, pupils, facial strength, neck flexion, and proximal limb strength
cranial nerve examination: asymmetrical fatigable ptosis; otherwise normal
sustained upgaze fatigability test: 'PRONOUNCED PTOSIS' on counting 1 to 100 - the right eye closed completely while the left droop increased
ocular motility examination: full in all directions
pupil examination (size, light reaction): equal and reactive
limb and neck power: neck weakness, extensors more than flexors
2. Ice-pack test applied to the more ptotic eyelid
ice-pack test: partial improvement
3. Serum acetylcholine-receptor antibody panel, including binding, blocking, and modulating antibodies
anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies: 16.63 nmol/L - elevated
4. Serum MuSK antibody
anti-MuSK antibodies: negative
5. Repetitive nerve-stimulation electromyography of facial and proximal limb muscles
repetitive nerve stimulation: decremental response in facial and spinal accessory nerves
6. Single-fiber electromyography with jitter measurement
single-fibre EMG: normal jitter
7. Serum creatine kinase level
creatine kinase: normal
8. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine levels
thyroid function (TSH, free T4): normal
9. Serum electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal function, and liver function
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
liver function tests: normal
serum calcium, magnesium and phosphate: normal
10. MRI of the brain and orbits with attention to the ocular motor nerves and extraocular muscles
MRI orbits: normal extraocular muscles, no mass
MRI brain with contrast: no lesion, no cranial nerve enhancement
11. CT scan of the chest with contrast
CT chest (thymus): no thymoma
12. Mitochondrial myopathy genetic testing if neuromuscular-junction studies and antibody testing are unrevealing
mitochondrial genetics (mtDNA deletion): no deletion
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Generalized seropositive myasthenia gravis (anti–acetylcholine receptor antibody–positive autoimmune neuromuscular-junction disease), without thymoma

ALTERNATIVES:  
1. MuSK-antibody-negative autoimmune myasthenia gravis with predominantly ocular and axial involvement  
2. Congenital myasthenic syndrome  
3. Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy
